q: What is data?
r: Facts, numbers or observations that can be recorded
Data becomes useful once it is organized.
w: Opinions that nobody has written down anywhere
Software that carries out instructions on a computer
Machines that store information inside a building

q: Which of these is quantitative data?
r: The number of customers who visited a store today
It is a count that can be measured as a number.
w: A customer's description of the store's atmosphere
The color of a store's front door
That is a category, not a measured number.
A customer's favorite flavor of ice cream
That is a category, not a measured number.

q: Which of these is qualitative data?
r: Written comments from a customer survey
They describe opinions in words rather than numbers.
w: The weight of a package in kilograms
The price of an item in dollars
The number of items sold in a week

q: What is the difference between structured and unstructured data?
r: Structured data fits tables with set fields; unstructured data does not
Emails and photos are common unstructured data.
w: Structured data is always larger than unstructured data
Size does not define the difference.
Structured data is only text while unstructured is only numbers
Both types can contain many formats.
Structured data is stored on paper while unstructured is digital

q: A spreadsheet of names, dates and order totals in labeled columns is an example of:
r: Structured data
Rows and columns follow a fixed layout.
w: Unstructured data lacks a fixed layout.
A spreadsheet is not a model.

q: What is a data source?
r: The place or system that data comes from
Examples include sensors, surveys and databases.
w: The final chart that presents the findings
The person who reads the final report
The rule that decides how data is stored
That describes a policy or format.

q: What is primary data?
r: Data a researcher collects directly for a specific purpose
A survey you run yourself creates primary data.
w: Data copied from a report someone else wrote
Data that is always numeric and exact
Primary data can be of any type.
Data that is stored in a cloud service

q: What is secondary data?
r: Data that was collected earlier by someone else
Government reports are common examples.
w: Data you collect yourself for the first time
Data that is less important than other data
Data that is stored in a backup file
Backups are copies, not a data type.

q: What does data quality mean?
r: How accurate, complete and consistent the data is
Poor quality leads to unreliable results.
w: How much storage the data uses
How fast the data can be copied
How colorful a chart of the data looks

q: Which problem makes a data set unreliable?
r: Many missing or incorrect values
Errors and gaps distort any analysis.
w: Documentation of where the data came from

q: What is data cleaning?
r: Finding and fixing errors, gaps and duplicates in a data set
Clean data gives better analysis.
w: Deleting all of the data to start again
Printing the data on clean paper

q: A table lists the same customer twice with identical details. What should an analyst do?
r: Remove the duplicate record
Duplicates can inflate counts and totals.
w: Keep both records to be safe
This would double count the customer.

q: A column of ages contains the value 250. What is the best first step?
r: Check whether it is an entry error and correct or remove it
A person cannot be 250 years old.
w: Leave it because all data is valid
Use it to compute the average without checking

q: What is a missing value?
r: An entry where no data was recorded
Blank cells are common examples.
w: A value that is the largest in a data set
A value that is repeated many times
A value that has been rounded

q: What is an outlier?
r: A value far from the rest of the data
It may be an error or a real unusual event.
w: A value that equals the average
A value that appears most often
A value that is exactly in the middle

q: Why should data be documented with a data dictionary?
r: It explains what each field means and how it is recorded
Users then interpret the data correctly.
w: It increases the size of the data on purpose
It deletes fields no one uses
It replaces the need for any column names

q: What is a database?
r: An organized collection of data that can be searched and updated
Many businesses store records in one.
w: A single chart showing sales over time
A device that connects to the internet

q: What is a primary key in a database table?
r: A field that uniquely identifies each record
No two rows share the same value.
w: A field that is always blank
A field that repeats in every row

q: Which field is the best primary key for a customer table?
r: A unique customer ID number
It is different for every customer.
w: Many customers share a first name.

q: What is big data?
r: Data sets so large or fast-changing that special tools are needed
Volume, velocity and variety describe it.
w: Any file larger than one megabyte
Size alone at that level is not big data.
Data that has been printed in large letters
Data that comes only from large companies
Source size is not the definition.

q: What are the three Vs of big data?
r: Volume, velocity and variety
They describe how much, how fast and how varied.
w: These are not the standard three.
These are not the standard three.
These are not the standard three.

q: What is a data set?
r: A collection of related data, often arranged in a table
It is the input for most analysis.
w: A tool that draws charts automatically
A rule that decides who may view data

q: What does it mean for data to be consistent?
r: It uses the same formats and units across records
Mixed formats cause errors in analysis.
w: It has never been changed by anyone
Consistency is about format, not history.
It is stored in a secret location

q: One column lists prices in dollars and another in euros without labels. Which data issue is this?
r: Inconsistent units
Mixed units lead to wrong comparisons.

q: What is probability?
r: A measure of how likely an event is to happen
It ranges from 0 to 1.
w: A measure of how large a group is
A measure of how fast a computer runs
A measure of how clear a chart looks

q: A probability of 0 means the event:
r: Cannot happen
Zero means impossible.
w: That would be a high probability.

q: A probability of 1 means the event:
r: Is certain to happen
One means certainty.

q: A fair coin is tossed once. What is the probability of heads?
r: Heads and tails are equally likely.
w: That would be two heads in a row.
That would mean heads is certain.

q: A bag holds 3 red and 7 blue marbles. What is the probability of drawing a red marble?
r: 3 out of 10 marbles are red.
w: That is the chance of blue.

q: What is the sum of probabilities of all possible outcomes?
r: Something in the full set must happen.
w: That would mean nothing can happen.
The total is always the same.

q: What is the probability of NOT rolling a 6 on a fair six-sided die?
r: It is 1 minus 1/6.
w: That is the chance of rolling a 6.

q: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability both land heads?
r: 1/2 times 1/2 equals 1/4.
w: That counts one head and one tail.

q: What is the mean of a data set?
r: The sum of values divided by how many there are
It is the usual average.
w: The value that appears most often
The largest value minus the smallest

q: What is the median of a data set?
r: The middle value when the data is sorted
It splits the data into two halves.
w: The sum of values divided by their count
The value that appears most often
The difference between highest and lowest

q: What is the mode of a data set?
r: The value that appears most often
A set can have more than one mode.
w: The middle value of the sorted data
That is the range or variance.

q: What is the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12?
r: The sum 40 divided by 5 equals 8.

q: What is the median of 3, 9, 4, 7 and 5?
r: Sorted values are 3, 4, 5, 7, 9, so the middle is 5.

q: What is the range of a data set?
r: The largest value minus the smallest value
It shows how spread out the data is.

q: A set of exam scores is 62, 70, 75, 88 and 95. What is the range?
r: 95 minus 62 equals 33.

q: What does standard deviation measure?
r: How spread out values are around the mean
A larger value means more variation.
w: How many values are in a set

q: Two classes have the same mean score. Class A has a small standard deviation and Class B a large one. What does this tell you?
r: Class B's scores are more spread out
A larger deviation means greater variation.
w: Class A's scores are more spread out
A small deviation means less spread.
Class A scored higher on average
Spread can differ with equal means.

q: What is a population in statistics?
r: The entire group you want to learn about
A sample is a part of it.
w: A small group chosen for study
The number of people in a city only

q: What is a sample in statistics?
r: A part of a population used to learn about the whole
Samples save time and cost.
w: A single value in a data set

q: Why is random sampling used?
r: It gives every member a fair chance of being chosen
This helps the sample represent the population.
w: It guarantees the sample is the biggest possible
It lets the researcher pick favorites
It removes the need for any data

q: A survey about school lunches only asks students eating in the cafeteria. What is the main problem?
r: Sampling bias, because other students are left out
The sample does not represent all students.
w: The issue is who was asked.
Clean data is not a problem.

q: What is correlation?
r: A relationship in which two variables tend to change together
It does not prove one causes the other.
w: A proof that one variable causes another
A random error in a data set

q: Ice cream sales and sunburn cases both rise in summer. What is the best conclusion?
r: They are correlated, but ice cream does not cause sunburn
Warm weather affects both.

q: What is a normal distribution?
r: A bell-shaped curve with most values near the mean
It is symmetric around the center.
w: A curve with all values equal
A scatter of random points with no pattern
That is not a defined shape.

q: In a normal distribution, about what share of values lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
r: About 68%
This is a standard rule of thumb.
w: That is for two standard deviations.

q: What is a hypothesis in a statistical test?
r: A claim about a population that can be tested with data
The data supports or fails to support it.
w: A proven fact that needs no testing

q: What does a small p-value (such as 0.01) suggest?
r: The result would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true
It gives evidence against the null hypothesis.
w: The null hypothesis is certainly true
A small p-value argues against it.
The sample is too small to use
The p-value does not measure size.

q: What is a confidence interval?
r: A range likely to contain the true value of a population measure
It reflects uncertainty from sampling.
w: A guarantee that the estimate is exact
It is a range, not an exact value.
The time needed to collect data
It is not a time measure.
The most common value in a sample
